# Reduced Working Time and Productivity: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

*Review of Work and Employment Research. S. Achterberg, N. Iwu, F. Castell and J. Moreno. Review protocol registered before search.*

## Abstract

We systematically reviewed studies of reductions in scheduled working time of at least 10% with pay maintained, reporting a quantitative measure of output. Twenty-three studies (1998–2025; about 41,000 workers) met inclusion criteria. Pooled across studies, output per hour rose by 13.4% (95% CI 8.1 to 19.0), with very high heterogeneity (I² = 81%). Output per worker changed by −1.8% (95% CI −4.9 to +1.4). Study design, the hours measure and the type of work explain much of the heterogeneity: controlled studies found smaller effects (+8.2%) than uncontrolled before–after studies (+18.7%), studies using actual hours found smaller effects (+7.9%) than those using scheduled hours (+16.6%), and per-worker output fell substantially in coverage-bound work (−8.9%) but not in discretionary work (+0.6%). There is evidence of small-study bias; adjusting for it reduces the pooled per-hour estimate to +9.1%. Effects show no sign of decay over time.

## Methods

**Search and inclusion.** We searched four bibliographic databases and two working-paper repositories, and contacted authors of known pilots. Studies were included if they (a) evaluated a reduction in scheduled hours of at least 10% with no reduction in pay; (b) reported output per worker or output per hour, or data from which either could be derived; and (c) had at least 50 workers. We excluded studies reporting only self-rated productivity. Of 412 records screened, 23 studies met the criteria.

**Outcomes.** The primary outcome is the change in output per hour, expressed as a log ratio and converted back to a percentage for reporting. Where a study reported both scheduled and actual hours, we used actual hours. The secondary outcome is the change in output per worker. For controlled studies we used the difference relative to the comparison group; for uncontrolled studies, the change from baseline.

**Coding of work type.** Two coders independently classified each study's setting as *discretionary* (output can be produced at any time within a deadline: case processing, professional services, software, back-office work), *coverage-bound* (output depends on staff being present while demand arrives: counters, contact centres, retail floors, care rotas), or *mixed/unclear*. Agreement was high (κ = 0.84); disagreements were resolved by discussion.

**Synthesis.** Random-effects meta-analysis with restricted maximum-likelihood estimation; moderators examined by meta-regression. Small-study effects assessed by funnel plot, Egger's regression test, and trim-and-fill.

## Included studies

Of the 23 studies, 9 had a comparison group (3 randomised, including the Varden County trial; 6 matched or difference-in-differences) and 14 were uncontrolled before–after designs, including the Halden multi-organisation pilot. Eight studies measured actual hours; 15 used scheduled hours only. Thirteen settings were coded discretionary, 7 coverage-bound and 3 mixed or unclear. Only two studies were in manufacturing, both in the mixed category. Follow-up ranged from 3 to 30 months (median 6). Output measures were record-based in 12 studies and manager-reported in 11.

## Results

### Pooled effects

Across all 23 studies, output per hour rose by 13.4% (95% CI 8.1 to 19.0; I² = 81%). Output per worker changed by −1.8% (95% CI −4.9 to +1.4; I² = 74%). The prediction interval for output per hour runs from −4% to +34%, meaning that a new study in an unknown setting could plausibly find anything from a small loss to a very large gain.

### Moderators

**Table 1. Subgroup estimates of the change in output per hour and output per worker**

| Subgroup | k | Output per hour | Output per worker |
|---|---|---|---|
| **All studies** | 23 | +13.4% (8.1 to 19.0) | −1.8% (−4.9 to +1.4) |
| Controlled designs | 9 | +8.2% (4.0 to 12.6) | −4.1% (−7.6 to −0.5) |
| Uncontrolled before–after | 14 | +18.7% (11.2 to 26.7) | −0.2% (−4.0 to +3.8) |
| Actual hours measured | 8 | +7.9% (3.6 to 12.4) | −3.9% (−7.8 to +0.1) |
| Scheduled hours only | 15 | +16.6% (9.9 to 23.7) | −0.6% (−4.3 to +3.3) |
| Record-based output | 12 | +9.7% (5.0 to 14.6) | −3.6% (−7.2 to +0.2) |
| Manager-reported output | 11 | +17.8% (10.0 to 26.1) | +0.4% (−3.9 to +4.9) |
| Discretionary work | 13 | +15.1% (8.8 to 21.8) | +0.6% (−2.8 to +4.1) |
| Coverage-bound work | 7 | +6.2% (1.1 to 11.6) | −8.9% (−13.1 to −4.5) |
| Mixed or unclear | 3 | +12.0% (−1.5 to 27.4) | −2.9% (−10.6 to +5.4) |

In a multiple meta-regression including design, hours measure and work type together, all three moderators remained associated with the effect, and together they explained 58% of between-study variance. The design and measurement moderators overlap heavily: 12 of the 14 uncontrolled studies used scheduled hours, and 9 of the 14 used manager-reported output. Our data cannot fully separate them.

The work-type moderator is the clearest for the per-worker outcome. In discretionary work, output per worker was essentially unchanged in pooled estimates; in coverage-bound work, it fell by about 9%, consistent across all seven studies (I² = 22%). The per-hour gain in coverage-bound work was real but too small to compensate for the hours lost.

Note that the discretionary estimate of +15.1% per hour mixes controlled and uncontrolled studies. Restricting to the five controlled discretionary studies, the per-hour estimate is +9.6% (4.8 to 14.6) and the per-worker estimate −2.7% (−6.5 to +1.2).

### Small-study effects

The funnel plot is asymmetric, with small studies reporting larger per-hour gains (Egger's test p = 0.02). Trim-and-fill imputes five missing studies on the left of the funnel and reduces the pooled per-hour estimate from +13.4% to +9.1% (95% CI 3.9 to 14.6). We interpret this as evidence that small, favourable pilots are more likely to be published or publicised than small, unfavourable ones.

### Duration

Four studies reported follow-up beyond 12 months. Their pooled per-hour gain was +14.0% (95% CI 6.2 to 22.4), indistinguishable from the overall estimate. Effects show no sign of decay, and novelty explanations can therefore be set aside.

### Mechanisms

Eleven studies measured fatigue or wellbeing alongside output. Across these, the study-level correlation between the improvement in fatigue scores and the per-hour gain was weak (r = 0.18). Only three studies measured time spent in meetings, and none tested meetings as a mediator under a registered plan; we cannot assess this mechanism. Sick leave fell in all 14 studies that reported it (pooled −31%), and staff turnover fell in all 9 that reported it.

## Discussion

The literature supports a gain in output per hour from reduced working time, but a considerably smaller one than headline pilots suggest. The figure most often quoted, a gain of more than 20%, comes from uncontrolled studies using scheduled hours and manager-reported output; each of those features is associated with larger estimates. Controlled studies, studies measuring actual hours, studies using records, and the bias-adjusted estimate converge on a gain of roughly 8 to 10%.

Whether that gain is "enough" depends on the type of work. In discretionary settings the evidence is compatible with output per worker being maintained or falling slightly; in coverage-bound settings it falls clearly, and maintaining service would require additional staff.

We do not find support for the claim, made in one re-analysis of the Halden pilot, that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact. The controlled and actual-hours subgroups, which avoid the problems that re-analysis identified, still show gains whose confidence intervals exclude zero. Nor do we find support for the claim that reduced hours are sector-general.

## Limitations

Twenty-three studies is a small base for a meta-regression with three correlated moderators. Most studies are short. Only nine are controlled, and the controlled studies are themselves mostly in the public sector. Manufacturing and shift-based production are almost absent. Classification of work type, though reliable between coders, imposes a binary on what is often a mix within a single organisation.

response:
# Critical Read: Achterberg et al., "Reduced Working Time and Productivity: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis"

**Bottom line:** This is a careful and mostly well-calibrated review. The protocol was registered, coding was done independently, heterogeneity is reported honestly, and the authors admit the moderators are confounded with each other. The central conclusion holds up: a real but modest gain in output per hour of roughly 8–10%, no gain in output per worker, and a clear loss where output depends on staff being present. The serious weakness is the **duration claim**. Four studies compared against the rest cannot show that "novelty explanations can be set aside." That is the mirror image of the Varga & Holm comment, which asserted novelty without evidence. There are also some methodological omissions that matter more than the authors suggest.

## Internal consistency checks

- **The pooled estimates fit together sensibly.** Output per hour and output per worker imply hours cuts of about 11–16% across subgroups. That is plausible given the ≥10% inclusion threshold and the gap between actual and scheduled hours.
- **The "convergence" claim holds.** Controlled designs (+8.2%), actual hours (+7.9%), record-based output (+9.7%), controlled discretionary studies (+9.6%) and the trim-and-fill estimate (+9.1%) all fall within 7.9–9.7%.
- **The design and measurement overlap can be partly reconstructed.** The paper says 12 of 14 uncontrolled studies used scheduled hours and 9 of 14 used manager reports. Working back from the subgroup counts, the 9 controlled studies include about 6 measuring actual hours and about 7 using records. So "controlled" and "better measured" largely describe the same studies.

## What it does well

- **It examines the right moderators.** Design, hours measure, output source and work type are exactly the issues raised by the earlier documents.
- **It reports a prediction interval (−4% to +34%).** This is more useful to an employer than the pooled mean, and it is often omitted.
- **It adopts the discretionary vs coverage-bound distinction** from Varden, codes it reliably (κ = 0.84), and finds it consistent across studies (I² = 22% in the coverage-bound group).
- **It flags its own mixed estimate.** It separates the +15.1% discretionary figure from the controlled-only +9.6%.
- **Its treatment of mechanisms is honest.** It reports a weak correlation with fatigue and declines to judge the meetings hypothesis on three studies.
- **Its response to Varga & Holm is measured.** The point is correct: the subgroups that avoid their criticisms still exclude zero.

## Problems

### 1. The duration conclusion is not supported
"Effects show no sign of decay, and novelty explanations can therefore be set aside" rests on four studies and has several problems:

- **It compares different studies, not the same studies over time.** The long-running studies may differ from the rest in design, hours measure or setting. If they are mostly uncontrolled with scheduled hours, +14.0% should be compared with +16.6–18.7%, not with +13.4%, and would then suggest some decline.
- **Survivorship.** Schemes that last beyond 12 months are disproportionately the ones that worked. In Halden, 5 organisations reverted and only 18 made the change permanent. Long follow-ups only exist where the scheme continued.
- **The confidence interval is wide.** A range of 6.2% to 22.4% is consistent with a meaningful decline from early estimates. "Indistinguishable" is not the same as "no decay."
- **Within-study trajectories are not reported.** A proper test would compare month 3 with month 12 within the same studies. Halden had monthly output data. Varden's 24-month follow-up is the obvious place to look.

The fair conclusion is "no evidence of decay, with weak power to detect it." Novelty remains an open question, not a dismissed one.

### 2. Size of the hours cut is not a moderator
For any given output change, a larger cut in hours mechanically produces a larger gain per hour. Studies ranged from cuts of at least 10% to 20% or more. Some of the moderator differences could therefore reflect cut size, for example if uncontrolled pilots tended to use bigger cuts. The review should either meta-regress on cut size or analyse an elasticity: the change in output relative to the change in hours.

### 3. No formal risk-of-bias assessment
Design and measurement are analysed as moderators, but no structured tool such as RoB 2, ROBINS-I or GRADE is reported. That matters because a moderator analysis cannot capture biases like the following:

- **Attrition.** Halden's misdescribed withdrawals are the clearest example. Did the review use Halden's reported +23.4% or the corrected figures from the microdata?
- **Selective reporting.** Sick leave "fell in all 14 studies that reported it." Were the studies that didn't report it the ones where it didn't fall?

### 4. Studies are classified as a whole, but some contain both types of work
Work type is coded per study. Varden has a randomised discretionary arm (+12.5% per hour) and a coverage-bound arm (+6.7%). Halden covers six sectors, including retail.

If Varden was coded "mixed," its key contrast was lost. If it was split, the study count would not be 23. The paper should say which, and ideally code each stratum separately.

### 5. Small-study bias is interpreted too confidently
- **The asymmetry may reflect study type, not unpublished studies.** Smaller studies are probably the uncontrolled pilots using scheduled hours. So the funnel asymmetry may reflect genuine differences between kinds of study rather than missing ones.
- **Trim-and-fill is unreliable when heterogeneity is high.** Here I² = 81%.
- **Adjustments may be stacked.** The +9.1% figure and the moderator-based estimates may correct for the same problem twice. They are not independent confirmations.

### 6. The abstract leads with the reassuring per-worker figure
The abstract's per-worker result is the pooled −1.8%, with a confidence interval that includes zero. The more reliable controlled estimate is −4.1% (−7.6 to −0.5), which excludes zero. A reader of the abstract alone would get a rosier view than the best evidence supports.

### 7. Manager reports are treated inconsistently
Self-rated productivity is excluded, but manager-reported output is included in 11 studies. Varga & Holm showed manager reports exceed the records by about 4 points. A sensitivity analysis excluding them would be the natural check; the record-based subgroup is a partial version of that.

### 8. The coverage-bound per-hour gain is called "real," but may partly reflect busier staff
With the same queue served by fewer staff, each person is idle less, and waits get longer. Part of the +6.2% may reflect fuller utilisation paid for by worse service, not more efficient work.

### 9. The best-quality subset is not reported
The most informative cell would be studies that are controlled, measure actual hours and use records. It probably contains about 5–6 studies. Reporting it would give the cleanest single estimate.

## How it fits with the earlier documents

| Question | Halden | Varden | Varga & Holm | This review |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Gain in output per hour | +23.4% | +12.5% (discretionary) / +6.7% (coverage) | ~11% residual, claimed artifact | ~8–10% (best estimates) |
| Output per worker, discretionary work | ~−1% | −2.1% (n.s.) | — | −2.7% (controlled, n.s.) |
| Output per worker, coverage-bound work | −6.9% (retail) | −11.4% | −11.2% (n = 3) | −8.9% |
| Durability | Asserted | 24-month follow-up pending | Asserted *against* | Asserted *for*, on weak evidence |
| Mechanism | Fatigue (untested) | Meetings (exploratory) | Rejects meetings | Fatigue weak; meetings untestable |

The documents now agree quite closely on the size of the effects. What remains unresolved is mainly **durability** and **mechanism**, and both sides have overclaimed on durability.

## A fair summary

Across 23 studies, cutting hours at full pay is associated with a gain in output per hour of roughly 8–10% in the better-designed and better-measured studies. Plausible values run from about 4% to 14%, and less than the 20%+ seen in headline pilots. In discretionary work, output per worker is roughly maintained, perhaps with a small loss of about 3%. In coverage-bound work it falls by about 9%, and service is maintained only with extra staff.

Whether the gains last is not established: the evidence on duration is too thin and too subject to survivorship to settle it either way. Why the gains occur (rest, fewer meetings, or both) is also unknown. Varden's 24-month follow-up, including its registered test of the meetings hypothesis, is the most important pending evidence.
